analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act in its entirety, restoring the law as it stood before.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in eight House committees until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the entire Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act — the law known as Obamacare — effective as if it had never passed, and restore all prior law. That would eliminate the law's coverage expansions, insurance rules, and tax provisions all at once. It was introduced within days of the Act becoming law, was referred to eight House committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households, who would stop paying the law's new Medicare taxes on investment income and high wages; insurers selling Medicare Advantage plans, which would regain payments the law reduced; brand-name drug makers, which would no longer owe the law's Medicare drug discounts; and medical device makers, which would avoid the law's excise tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, Medicare Advantage insurers, drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act in full, effective as of its enactment, and restores every provision of law that the Act amended or repealed. [S2] [S3]
Restoring the prior law would undo the Act's tax and revenue provisions, which fell mainly on higher-income households and specific industries such as drug and device makers. [S3]
Because the repeal is total and contains no replacement, it would also strip the Act's insurance market rules and coverage programs — an all-or-nothing approach. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who had just gained under the new law: people who could not get affordable insurance before, young adults allowed to stay on a parent's plan, seniors receiving help with drug costs, and people with pre-existing conditions whom insurers could again refuse or charge more. The federal government would also lose the revenue the Act raised.
analysis.who_pays_short: People who had just gained coverage and protections

drawbacks.text: A full repeal would remove the Act's insurance protections, coverage expansions and help with drug costs, returning the health insurance market to the rules in place before the Act. [S2] [S3]
Repealing the Act would also erase the revenue it raised, increasing deficits unless offset — which this bill does not do. [S3]
Supporters argued the Act raised premiums and imposed mandates and new taxes on employers and households; this bill offered no replacement provisions to address those concerns. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow mostly to higher-income households and to drug, device and Medicare Advantage interests through tax and payment rollbacks, while the largest cost — losing new coverage expansions and insurance protections — falls on ordinary people, particularly the sick and lower-income. Because it repeals without replacing, even its supporters' cost concerns were left unaddressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees and then to subcommittees, but no committee ever acted on it and the House never voted before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 22, 2010, at the moment the Affordable Care Act was completing enactment. [S1] [S5]

It was referred the same day to eight committees — Energy and Commerce plus Appropriations, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration and Rules — with the timing of consideration left to the Speaker. [S3] [S5]

Within a week parts of it were sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Education and Labor Health subcommittee, and no further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the Congress. [S5]
Its only support on the record was its sponsor and 12 Republican cosponsors in a House where Democrats held 253 of 435 seats. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who had just gained coverage and protections under the new health care law kept them; health insurers kept the new subsidized customer base the Act created, and brand-name drug makers and high-income households remained on the hook for the Act's taxes and discounts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who kept the new law's coverage and protections

for.name: Rep. Jerry Moran
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill two days after final action on the Affordable Care Act and gave introductory remarks on the House floor. [S1] [S5]

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: As Speaker, controlled the referral and scheduling process; the bill was referred to eight committees with consideration timing left to her, and it was never brought to the floor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Lead committee of referral, then chaired by Henry Waxman (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent it to its Health Subcommittee, where it remained without a hearing or markup. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican — 13 of 178 House Republicans — while Democrats held 253 of 435 House seats and no Democrat supported the bill; the Democratic majority let it die in committee.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from the Act's medical loss ratio, rating and coverage rules, but would also strip away the mandate-backed customer base and subsidies that route coverage dollars through them. Insurers largely defended the Act after enactment because of those guaranteed customers.

The Act required brand-name makers to provide 50% discounts for seniors in the Medicare coverage gap and opened the market to cheaper biosimilars; repeal would erase both obligations, restoring the prior status quo at seniors' and taxpayers' expense.
Repeal would eliminate the Act's excise tax on medical devices, sparing the industry a cost that would otherwise fund coverage expansions.
The Act reduced payments to Medicare Advantage plans; repeal would restore the higher payments, meaning taxpayers and traditional Medicare pay more for the same coverage.
Repeal would erase the Act's Medicare taxes on high wages and investment income, a direct tax cut concentrated at the top that also removes funding for the coverage expansions.
